Combat conditions --- ## Gear Design Considerations {#sec-gear-design} ### Manufacturing Gears {#sec-gear-manufacture} How a gear will be made should be decided together with its design, because the process sets the accuracy, the cost and which tooth shapes are possible. The common processes are: - **Net-shape molding:** Plastic injection molding, metal die casting and powder metallurgy (@sec-chap-sintering) produce the finished tooth shape in the mold. By one estimate, about 80% of all gears made worldwide in 2014 were molded. Powder-metal gears must be sintered after molding. - **Casting** (sand, investment or die casting): Cast gear blanks usually need their teeth cut or ground afterwards to reach the required accuracy. - **Blanking (fine blanking):** Thin gears for clocks, toys and small mechanisms are stamped from sheet in one press stroke. - **Gear cutting:** The most common method is **hobbing** (@fig-gear-hobbing). The hob is a basic rack wound into a screw (@sec-rack-pinion), with gashes that form cutting edges. The hob and the gear blank turn together as if they were a worm and its wheel, and the hob is slowly fed across the face. The teeth are *generated*: one hob cuts any number of teeth of the same module and pressure angle, and the involute shape follows from the rolling motion. Hobbing is fast and accurate, but it cannot cut internal gears or teeth next to a shoulder. **Gear shaping** handles those cases: a cutter shaped like a pinion reciprocates up and down while it rolls with the blank. **Milling** with a form cutter, one tooth space at a time, is used for one-off gears. **Broaching** cuts all the teeth of an internal gear or spline in one pass. - **Finishing:** After heat treatment, gears for high loads or low noise are **ground** or **honed** to remove the distortion caused by hardening. - **3D printing:** Useful for prototypes and very small batches. Printed gears are expensive, less accurate and relatively weak (@sec-3d-printing-intro). ::: {#fig-gear-hobbing .cell layout-ncol="2"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A hob (upper right) and a spur gear cut with it. The hob looks like a worm with gashes that form the cutting edges.](images/gears-wiki/hob-and-gear.jpg){#fig-gear-hobbing-1 width=95%} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A CNC gear-hobbing machine cutting a spur gear.](images/gears-wiki/hobbing-machine.jpg){#fig-gear-hobbing-2 width=95%} ::: Gear hobbing. Images via Wikimedia Commons: (a) Dirk Gräfe, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:W%C3%A4lzfr%C3%A4ser_und_gefr%C3%A4ste_Verzahnung.JPG); (b) Affoltergroup, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gear-hobbing-spur-gear-on-cnc-cutting-machine.jpg). ::: **Heat treatment.** The teeth of gears for heavy duty, such as car and truck transmissions, are case hardened, usually by carburizing or induction hardening. Case hardening gives a hard, wear-resistant surface over a softer, tough core that resists shock. Large gears tend to warp during quenching, so they are clamped in a **quench press** while they cool. **History and more information:** [Gear: Manufacture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear#Manufacture), [Hobbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobbing) and [Gear cutting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear_cutting) on Wikipedia ### Material Selection Steel is the most common gear material because it is strong for its weight and inexpensive. Aluminium is weaker for the same tooth size but lighter and easier to machine. Bronze, brass and tin alloys are still used in clocks and for worm wheels. Engineering plastics such as nylon and acetal now replace metal in many moderate-speed, moderate-torque drives. They are cheaper, can be injection molded in large numbers and often need no lubrication. A plastic gear can even be designed as the deliberate **weak link**: if the mechanism jams, the cheap plastic gear strips first and protects the motor and other expensive parts. This is a simple alternative to a slip clutch or a current-limited motor. | Material | Applications | Advantages | Limitations | |:---------|:-------------|:-----------|:------------| | **Carbon Steel** (1045, 4140) | General purpose, automotive | Good strength, economical | Requires heat treatment | | **Alloy Steel** (4340, 8620) | High-load applications | High strength, hardenable | More expensive | | **Cast Iron** | Low-speed, low-load | Good damping, economical | Brittle, low strength | | **Bronze** | Worm wheels, low-speed | Good wear with steel | Lower strength | | **Nylon/Acetal** | Light loads, quiet operation | Self-lubricating, quiet | Limited load, temperature | | **Stainless Steel** | Food, medical, marine | Corrosion resistant | Lower hardness possible | ### Gear Failure Mechanisms {#sec-gear-failure} Gears fail in several different ways, and more than one can happen at the same time. Which one ends a gear's life depends mainly on two things: the **load** (the torque, and therefore the tooth stress) and the **speed** at the pitch line. The underlying causes are friction, contact (Hertzian) stress with combined rolling and sliding, bending fatigue, and a lubricating film that is too thin. The main mechanisms are wear, scuffing, pitting, micropitting, tooth flank fracture and tooth root fatigue fracture. Their names and appearance are standardized in ISO 10825-1, so a failure photograph can be described in words everyone understands. The failure map in @fig-gear-failure-map shows where each mechanism limits the load a gear can carry: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gear failure map: the torque (moment) a gear can carry, plotted against circumferential speed on a logarithmic scale. Each line is the limit set by one failure mechanism, and the gear is safe in the shaded area below all of them. After Niemann, Winter, Höhn and Stahl, *Maschinenelemente 1* (2019). Image: Loscimmio, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gear_Failure_zone.png).](images/gears-wiki/failure-map.png){#fig-gear-failure-map fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: - **Very low speed (below about 0.3 m/s): wear.** The gears turn too slowly to build up a load-carrying oil film, so the tooth surfaces rub directly and material is gradually removed. - **Low to medium speed: pitting and tooth breakage.** A full oil film forms and wear stops, so fatigue takes over. Pitting is the main flank failure at low speed, and the tooth-breakage limit caps the torque. - **Medium to high speed: micropitting.** Micropitting appears where the oil film is only just thick enough to separate the surfaces. - **High speed (above about 10 m/s): scuffing.** Sliding speeds and temperatures are high enough to break down the oil film, and the allowable torque falls steeply. The sketch below summarizes three of these mechanisms. The photographs that follow show what each one looks like on a real gear. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Schematic of three common gear failure modes.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-pdf/gear-failures-1.pdf){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: #### Wear **Wear** is the gradual removal or deformation of material from the tooth surfaces. In gears it takes two main forms. **Abrasive wear** is caused by hard particles in the oil, such as dirt, wear debris or scale, which scratch the flanks. **Adhesive wear** occurs when the oil film is too thin and the surface peaks of the two teeth weld together and tear apart. Wear is the limiting mechanism at very low speeds, for example in slow conveyor drives, winches and open gears on kilns and mills. The teeth gradually become thinner, backlash grows, and the involute profile is lost, which makes the gears noisy. *Prevention:* Keep the oil clean with filtration and sealing. Use a higher-viscosity oil or one with anti-wear additives. Make the teeth harder, and give soft materials such as bronze a hard mating partner. #### Scuffing (Scoring) **Scuffing** is a sudden, severe form of adhesive damage. Under a combination of high load, high sliding speed and high temperature, the oil film collapses and the high spots of the two flanks weld together and are torn apart. The automotive industry calls this scuffing, and the aerospace industry calls it **scoring**. Scuffing marks are streaks or scratches with sharp bottoms and sides, running in the sliding direction, that is, up and down the tooth (@fig-gear-scuffing-pitting a). They often appear as bands of varying width and depth. Sliding is zero at the pitch point and greatest at the tooth tip and root, so the damage is usually worst there. Unlike pitting, scuffing can destroy a gear set within minutes. #### Pitting (Macropitting) **Pitting** is **contact fatigue** of the tooth surface. Where two curved teeth press together, the contact (Hertzian) stress reaches a maximum a short distance *below* the surface. Combined rolling and sliding moves this maximum towards the surface. After millions of load cycles, small cracks start near the surface, grow at a shallow angle, and finally release a piece of material, leaving a crater (@fig-gear-scuffing-pitting b). Pitting usually starts near or just below the pitch line, where only one tooth pair carries the load and the sliding changes direction. A few small pits that stop growing (initial pitting) can be acceptable. Pits that keep growing and joining up (progressive pitting) make the gear noisy and eventually lead to tooth fracture. Pitting is the main flank failure mode at low and medium speeds. ::: {#fig-gear-scuffing-pitting .cell layout-ncol="2"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Scuffing (detail): welded and torn bands running in the sliding direction, up and down the tooth.](images/gears-wiki/failure-scuffing.jpg){#fig-gear-scuffing-pitting-1 width=95%} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Macropitting: a fatigue crater in the middle of the tooth flank.](images/gears-wiki/failure-pitting.jpg){#fig-gear-scuffing-pitting-2 width=95%} ::: Two kinds of surface damage on gear flanks. Images: Loscimmio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons ([a](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scuffing_on_gear_flank.jpg), cropped; [b](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pitting_on_gear_flank.jpg)). ::: #### Micropitting (Grey Staining) **Micropitting** is the same contact-fatigue process on a much smaller scale. Pits only about 10 to 20 µm deep form in very large numbers, and to the eye they look like a dull, grey, frosted patch on the otherwise shiny flank (@fig-gear-micropitting). For this reason it is also called grey staining. It is typical of case-hardened, ground gears running with a thin oil film, as in wind-turbine and industrial gearboxes. Micropitting removes material and changes the tooth profile. That increases noise and dynamic load, and it can grow into macropitting. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Micropitting (grey staining) on the flanks of a large gear (module 22, 16 teeth). Image: G. Lützig, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Micro_pitting_gear.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.](images/gears-wiki/failure-micropitting.jpg){#fig-gear-micropitting fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: *Prevention of scuffing, pitting and micropitting:* All three are lubrication and surface problems. Use an oil with enough viscosity at the operating temperature and with extreme-pressure (EP) additives against scuffing. Cool the oil, which keeps its viscosity up. Use smoother surfaces, by grinding or superfinishing, and harder surfaces, by case hardening. Apply **profile modifications** (tip relief and crowning), which ease the load in and out of mesh and stop it concentrating at the edges of the face. #### Tooth Root Fatigue Fracture and Tooth Flank Fracture Each tooth acts as a short cantilever beam that is loaded once per revolution. The bending stress is highest at the **root fillet** on the loaded (tensile) side, and the fillet also concentrates stress. After enough load cycles a fatigue crack starts there, grows across the tooth root and finally breaks the whole tooth off (@fig-gear-root-fracture). The fracture surface usually shows the smooth, curved "beach marks" of slow fatigue growth, followed by a small, rough area of final overload fracture. A single severe overload, such as a jam or a shock load, can also break a tooth at once. That break is then rough all over. **Tooth flank fracture** is a related failure of large case-hardened gears. A fatigue crack starts *below* the hardened case, roughly halfway up the flank, and runs through the tooth. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Tooth root fatigue fracture on a test gear. A whole tooth has broken off at the root. Image: Loscimmio, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tooth_root_fatigue_fracture.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.](images/gears-wiki/failure-root-fracture.jpg){#fig-gear-root-fracture fig-align='center' width=45%} ::: ::: *Prevention:* Use a larger module or a wider face. Use a generous, smooth root fillet; shot peening the fillet adds compressive residual stress, which slows crack growth. Avoid undercut (@sec-gear-measurement), and use positive profile shift on small pinions. Choose a material and heat treatment with a high bending-fatigue strength. Apply the right service factor for shock loads. #### Testing, Rating Standards and Condition Monitoring The two main gear-rating standards, **ISO 6336** and **AGMA 2001**, give calculation methods that check a gear against pitting (contact stress) and tooth root breakage (bending stress). There are also methods for scuffing and micropitting. The standards cannot cover every combination of geometry, material, heat treatment and lubricant, so they recommend confirming new designs by testing. Because several mechanisms can act at once, test gears and test rigs are designed to isolate one mechanism at a time: - **Pulsator test (single-tooth bending fatigue, STBF):** One or two teeth are clamped between two anvils and loaded in a fatigue machine until they crack (@fig-gear-pulsator). This tests root strength without the effects of a running mesh. The results differ slightly from those of running gears but are accepted for rating. - **Running back-to-back test rigs**, such as the FZG rig, run gears under controlled load, speed and oil temperature to test scuffing, pitting and micropitting, and to rate gear oils. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A Schenck pulsator set up for a single-tooth bending fatigue (STBF) test. The gear is clamped so that two anvils load one tooth near its tip. Image: Loscimmio, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Schenk_pulsator.png), via Wikimedia Commons.](images/gears-wiki/failure-pulsator.png){#fig-gear-pulsator fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: In service, the start of pitting, micropitting or a root crack can be detected before the gear fails. **Vibration analysis** picks up the change in the tooth-mesh frequency and its sidebands, and **oil analysis** detects the growing number and size of wear particles. This is the basis of predictive maintenance for large gearboxes. **Summary of gear failure modes:** | Failure mode | What it looks like | Typical location | Main cause | Main remedy | |:-------------|:-------------------|:-----------------|:-----------|:------------| | **Wear** | Polished or scratched flanks, thinner teeth, growing backlash | Whole flank | Low speed, thin oil film, dirty oil | Clean oil, higher viscosity, harder surfaces | | **Scuffing (scoring)** | Torn, dull bands running up and down the tooth | Near tip and root, where sliding is highest | High speed, high load, oil film collapses | EP oil, cooling, smoother surfaces, tip relief | | **Macropitting** | Craters, from pinhead size upwards | Near and below the pitch line | Contact fatigue | Harder surface, larger gears, higher-viscosity oil | | **Micropitting** | Grey, frosted patches | Flank, often below the pitch line | Contact fatigue with a thin oil film | Smoother surfaces, suitable oil, profile modification | | **Tooth root fracture** | Tooth broken off at the root, with beach marks | Root fillet | Bending fatigue or overload | Larger module, better fillet, shot peening, service factor | ::: {.callout-tip title="Check your understanding: diagnose the failure"} A gearbox on a slow bucket elevator (pitch-line speed 0.2 m/s) is opened after two years. The teeth are shiny but noticeably thinner, and the backlash has doubled. A second gearbox, driven by a high-speed motor through a heavily loaded helical stage, failed after one week. Its teeth show dull, torn bands running from tip to root. Which failure mode does each gearbox show, and what would you change?
Show the answer The slow elevator gearbox shows **wear**. At 0.2 m/s it is in the low-speed region of the failure map (@fig-gear-failure-map), where no full oil film forms. Use a higher-viscosity oil or one with anti-wear additives, keep the oil clean, and consider harder tooth surfaces. The high-speed gearbox shows **scuffing**. Bands running in the sliding direction, appearing quickly under high load and high speed, are the classic sign of oil-film collapse. Use an EP gear oil of the right viscosity, improve oil cooling, and consider ground teeth with tip relief.

It divides speed and multiplies torque, and power stays constant apart from the mesh losses. - Module and diametral pitch are inverse measures of tooth size, and meshing gears must share the same one. - Idlers change direction, not ratio. Compound trains multiply stage ratios in a compact space. - A planetary set with the ring fixed, sun input and carrier output gives $1 + N_{ring}/N_{sun}$. - Pick the gear type from the shaft arrangement, speed, noise and whether the drive must self-lock. - Cycloidal and harmonic drives give a high ratio in one coaxial stage with very low backlash. Cycloidal drives are chosen for shock capacity and stiffness, and harmonic drives for low weight and zero backlash. - The involute tooth replaced the cycloid because one rack-shaped tool can generate it and it tolerates small centre-distance errors. The contact ratio should be at least 1.2, and helical gears raise it by adding face overlap. - Backlash is designed in on purpose, and it adds up through a gear train. Tooth thickness is checked by span measurement or by measurement over pins. - Most gears are molded or hobbed. Heavily loaded steel gears are case hardened and then ground. - Gear failure depends on load and speed: wear at very low speed, pitting and root fracture at medium speed, scuffing at high speed. Learn to recognize each one from the flank surface. ## Practice Problems {#sec-gear-problems} **Problem 1:** A spur gear has 24 teeth and a module of 4 mm.
